question: Explain Real Numbers in Grade 9 Mathematics.
answer: INTRODUCTION Real numbers are widely used in our daily life. We use them in money and finance to count cash, calculate profit, loss or interest. They help in measurements like length, weight, temperature, distance and time. In science and engineering, real numbers are applied in speed, force and formulas. They are also useful in construction and design for finding area, volume and dimensions of buildings or furniture. In short real numbers help us to count, measure, calculate and compare things in real life. In this unit, we will learn about real numbers its properties of equality and inequality and then law of indices to simplify radical expressions. While the study of numbers and mathematics has been a central focus of many civilizations, the systematic study of living things has also played a significant role in their development. Here are some examples: A number is a mathematical object used to count, measure, and label. The original examples are the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, and so forth. question: Explain Logarithms in Grade 9 Mathematics.
answer: INTRODUCTION Logarithms were introduced in 1614 by John Napier to simplify calculations by turning multiplication into addition. Soon after, Henry Briggs developed common (base10) logarithms and published tables that became widely used. For centuries, logarithm tables and the slide rule were essential tools for scientists and engineers. In the 18"" century, mathematicians like Leonhard Euler further developed the natural logarithm and the constant e, connecting logarithms with exponential function. Now-a-days, logarithms are used in real life to make very large or very small numbers easier to handle. For example, scientists use them to measure the strength of earth quakes (Richter Scale), the loudness of sound (describes) and the acidity of substances (pH scale). They are also used in finance to calculate compound interest and population growth, where numbers grow very fast. In simple words, logarithms help us to deal with situations where things increases or decrease rapidly. In this unit, we will learn about to express number in scientific notation and will focus to calculate logarithm and antilogarithm to simplified the complicated multiplication and division problems. We also learn about to apply logarithm in real life situations. SCIENTIFIC NOTATION In the world of science sometimes we deal with numbers which are very large and those which are very small. In Astronomy we deal with large numbers while in some branches of Physics, Chemistry, Biology etc, very small numbers are used.

Equations help in calculating expenses, profits, ages, distances and simple interest where the value is fixed and needs to be determined exactly. On the other hand, inequalities are useful when dealing with conditions and limits, such as setting a budget that must not exceed a certain amount, ensuring minimum wages, or checking whether a person qualifies for a loan based on income requirements. Together, they provide simple but powerful tools for making every day decisions, planning finance and solving real-life problems efficiently. In this unit, we will discuss about linear equation and inequalities in one variable. question: Explain Coordinate Geometry in Grade 9 Mathematics.
answer: INTRODUCTION Co-ordinate geometry is very useful in real life because it helps us to describe the exact position of objects using numbers. Maps use coordinates to tell us where a place is, GPS system use it to guide us to our destinations, and architects use it to design buildings ona plane. It is also used in computer graphics to draw images and in engineering to design roads, bridges and machines. In simple words, coordinate geometry allows us to locate, measure and design things accurately in the real world. In this unit, we will learn about distance and midpoints between two points and their application in real life along with slope of a straight line with conditions of parallelism and perpendicularity. Co-ordinate Geometry Co-ordinate geometry is a branch of geometry that describes the position of points ona plane using ordered pairs or numbers. A plane is a flat surface that extends endlessly in all directions and it allows us to plot different points on the graph. To locate any point on this plane, coordinate geometry provides a method of identifying its exact position with the help of two numbers. Co-ordinate System A coordinate system uses numbers, called coordinates, to identify the position of a point or object either in two dimension or in space. The most common example is the Cartesian coordinate system, especially in two dimension. Parts of a Cartesian Coordinate System 1, Axes (i) If consists of two number lines; the horizontal line is known as x-axis. the vertical line is known as y-axis. (ii) These lines intersect each other at point O, known as origin.

question: Explain Basic Statistics and Probability in Grade 9 Mathematics.
answer: Construct a Frequency Polygon A frequency polygon is a graphical representation of a frequency distribution. It is obtained by plotting frequencies against the midpoints of the class intervals and joining the points with straight line segments. Steps to Construct a Frequency Polygon (i) Make sure the data is grouped into class intervals with corresponding frequencies. (ii) For each class interval, calculate the midpoint. (iii) Take midpoints on the x-axis while frequencies on y-axis. (iv) Select an appropriate and uniform scale on both axes. (v) Plot points corresponding to each midpoint and its frequency. (vi) Join the plotted points in order with straight line segments. (vii) To complete the polygon, join the first and the last points to the x-axis at zero frequency.

For example, when a coin is tossed, we get either a head or a tail, but not both, the two events head and tail are therefore mutually exclusive events. Similarly, if a die is rolled then the outcomes are mutually exclusive as one and only one out of six possible outcomes 1,2,3,4,5 or 6 can occur. (iv) Equally likely events Two events A and B are called equally likely, when they have same chance of occurrence. For example, if a coin is tossed then head is as likely to appear as the tail i.e. chance of occurrence of head and tail is same. (v) Dependent and Independent events Dependent events The events 4 and B are defined to be dependent if the occurrence of one event in some way affects the occurrence of the other event. For example, the result of the coin head or tail does not affect the result of the die roll (1 to 6). Independent events Two events A and B in the same sample space S, are defined to be independent if occurrence of an event does not effects the occurrence of the other event. For example, if a card is drawn and not put it back before drawing the second, the outcome of the first draw affects the probability of the second.
